title: Everyday Psychology
subtitle: Spot thinking traps and decide better

cards.prompt: You mainly seek out and remember information that confirms what you already believe.
cards.note: For every firm opinion, ask which observation would change your mind, then go looking for it. It is uncomfortable, but it protects you from costly mistakes.

cards.prompt: People who know little about a topic often overestimate their skill the most.
cards.note: Strong confidence early on is not a reliable sign of skill. Get feedback early from people who have truly mastered the field.

cards.prompt: You keep going with something hopeless because you have already put so much into it.
cards.note: Ask yourself: would I start this today if I were beginning from zero? What is already spent will not come back either way.

cards.prompt: Cue, routine, reward: the pattern behind every habit.
cards.note: To change a habit, keep the cue and the reward and swap only the routine. For example, a short walk instead of your phone when you get bored.

cards.prompt: Total absorption in a task that challenges you just right, and your sense of time disappears.
cards.note: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi described it: flow happens when challenge and skill are in balance. If you are bored, make the task harder; if you are overwhelmed, break it down.

cards.prompt: The first number you hear shapes your estimate, even if it is completely arbitrary.
cards.note: In negotiations it pays to name the first number yourself. When someone sets an anchor for you, consciously ask what you would have guessed without it.

cards.prompt: Losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains feel good.
cards.note: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky described this in their prospect theory. When fear of losing freezes you, write the upsides and downsides side by side.

cards.prompt: As soon as you know the outcome, you feel you knew it all along.
cards.note: Before important decisions, write down what you expect and why. That way you learn from what you actually knew, not from a flattering memory.

cards.prompt: One striking good trait, such as good looks, colours your judgement of everything else.
cards.note: Judge people and things on separate, specific criteria. When hiring, it helps to rate one question across all candidates before moving on to the next.

cards.prompt: What comes to mind easily seems more common than it is, for example plane crashes.
cards.note: Look at numbers instead of headlines when judging risk. Per kilometre, cars are far more dangerous than planes, even though crashes get more attention.

cards.prompt: After five reds at roulette, you believe black is now due.
cards.note: Independent events have no memory. The ball does not know what came before; the odds are the same on every spin.

cards.prompt: You learn about something new and then suddenly see it everywhere.
cards.note: The thing has not become more common; your attention just filters differently. Use it on purpose: name a goal clearly and you start noticing matching opportunities.

cards.prompt: You believe others notice your stain or slip of the tongue far more than they do.
cards.note: In one study, people wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed half the room noticed; in fact it was about a quarter. Most people are busy thinking about themselves.

cards.prompt: Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
cards.note: Give yourself short, fixed time boxes, say 25 minutes for a round of email. The work adapts surprisingly often.

cards.prompt: Unfinished tasks stay on your mind longer than finished ones.
cards.note: Before you stop for the day, write down open items and plan the next concrete step. It calms your mind almost as if the task were done.

cards.prompt: The same information feels different depending on wording: "90% survive" versus "10% die".
cards.note: Phrase important decisions to yourself once positively and once negatively. If your judgement shifts, the frame was steering you, not the facts.

cards.prompt: Once people agree to a small request, they are more likely to agree to a big one.
cards.note: You can use it on yourself: start a new habit ridiculously small, say a single push-up. The first yes makes the next step easier.

cards.prompt: You feel obliged to return a favour, even one you never asked for.
cards.note: That is why free samples exist. When you feel the pull, ask whether you would have said yes without the gift.

cards.prompt: Whatever is scarce or might soon be gone suddenly seems more valuable.
cards.note: "Only 2 rooms left!" is often pure sales design. Give yourself a night to think before bigger purchases; genuine deals usually survive that.

cards.prompt: You follow what many others are doing, especially when you are unsure.
cards.note: Use it for yourself by spending time with people who already live the way you want to. With reviews and queues, though, take a second, critical look.

cards.prompt: You value things you own more highly than the same item in a shop.
cards.note: When decluttering, ask: would I buy this today at this price? If not, it can go.

cards.prompt: You put other people's behaviour down to their character and underrate the circumstances.
cards.note: When someone cuts you off in traffic, think of three harmless reasons, such as an emergency. You will usually be closer to the truth and less annoyed.

cards.prompt: You regularly plan too little time, even though experience should have taught you better.
cards.note: Don't estimate from your gut; check how long similar projects really took in the past. Then add a buffer on top.

cards.prompt: The more decisions you have already made today, the worse your next ones become.
cards.note: How strong the effect really is remains debated in research. Still, making important calls early and automating small stuff like breakfast or clothes never hurts.

cards.prompt: Too many options make you less satisfied and freeze the decision.
cards.note: Limit yourself on purpose, say to three candidates, and take the first option that meets your criteria. "Good enough" often makes you happier than "the best".

cards.prompt: You pass up a small reward now to get a bigger one later.
cards.note: It became famous through the marshmallow test. It gets easier when you move the temptation out of sight instead of relying on willpower alone.

cards.prompt: You would rather stick with what you know, even when a change would be better.
cards.note: That is why defaults are so powerful. Set up your own so that doing nothing leads somewhere good, such as a standing order into a savings account.

cards.prompt: In a crowd, everyone helps less because they all assume someone else will.
cards.note: In an emergency, address one person directly: "You in the red jacket, call 112!" That makes someone feel personally responsible.

cards.prompt: You feel you don't deserve your success and fear being exposed as a fraud.
cards.note: Keep a list of concrete wins and the feedback others have given you. Facts on paper hold up better against the feeling than brooding does.

cards.prompt: Simply encountering something often makes you like it more.
cards.note: That is why adverts run so often. The flip side: you can get used to new things like vegetables or exercise simply by repeating them regularly.
